Only if the negligence was intentional
Only in cases of death, not disablement
questions.src: Settled principle — Act excludes ordinary tort defences (contributory negligence, common employment, volenti non fit injuria) except for the specific statutory exceptions in Section 3(1) proviso

Only if the ESI claim is rejected first
Only for permanent disablement, not temporary

questions.q: An employee is crossing a public road just outside the factory gate, on her way to work, when she is struck by a passing vehicle unconnected to her employer's business. Applying the recognised exception to the Doctrine of Notional Extension, is the employer liable to pay compensation?
o: Yes, automatically, since the accident occurred near the workplace

No — where an accident occurs on a public road/place and the risk suffered arises from being a member of the public generally (not specifically from the employment), the notional extension doctrine does NOT apply, regardless of physical proximity to the workplace
Yes, because notional extension always covers the entire commute to and from work
No, because notional extension never applies to any accident outside the factory's physical boundary walls
questions.src: Settled exception to the Doctrine of Notional Extension — accidents on public roads/places where the risk is a general public risk (not specifically employment-related) fall outside the doctrine even if geographically proximate to the workplace; a frequently tested distinction from the general 'commute is covered' misconception

questions.q: Under Section 3(1) of the Employee's Compensation Act 1923, courts have interpreted the term used in the section as 'employment' rather than 'work' when determining the scope of notional extension. What is the significance of this specific word choice?
o: It has no legal significance — the two words are treated as interchangeable

'Employment' is interpreted more broadly than the narrower word 'work' would be, allowing the doctrine to cover activities and circumstances connected with the employment relationship even when the employee is not actively performing physical work duties at that exact moment
It means only physical labour counts, excluding any administrative or supervisory employees
It restricts compensation exclusively to injuries during actual working hours with no extension whatsoever
questions.src: Settled judicial interpretation of Section 3(1) — courts have specifically noted the statute uses 'employment' (broader) rather than 'work' (narrower), which is the textual foundation enabling the notional extension doctrine's expansive scope

questions.topic: ESI Act — Relationship with Employee's Compensation Act
questions.q: An employee's monthly wages are ₹19,000 (within the ESI wage ceiling), and their employer has 12 employees (above the ESI coverage threshold), but the employer has NOT actually registered the establishment or the employee under the ESI Act as legally required. If the employee suffers a workplace injury, what is the most accurate legal position?
o: The employee has no remedy at all since the employer failed to register

The employee remains statutorily COVERED under the ESI Act by operation of law (since the wage/establishment thresholds are met) despite the employer's default in registering — the employer's failure to comply does not deprive the employee of ESI coverage, and the employer may additionally face penalties for non-registration
The employee can only claim under the Employee's Compensation Act since ESI registration was never completed
The employee must personally register with ESIC before any claim can be made
questions.src: Settled ESI Act principle — coverage arises by operation of law once the statutory thresholds (wage ceiling, establishment size) are met; an employer's failure to register does not defeat the employee's entitlement, and non-registration itself is a separate penal default by the employer

questions.q: An employee completes exactly 4 years and 240 days of continuous service before resigning. Under the Payment of Gratuity Act 1972's settled interpretation of 'continuous service' for the 5-year eligibility threshold, is this employee generally entitled to gratuity?
o: No, since the employee has not completed a full 5 calendar years of service under any circumstances

Under the Act's definition of continuous service (Section 2A), an employee who has worked for at least 240 days in the preceding 12 months of the final year is generally deemed to have completed a full year of continuous service for that year — meaning 4 years plus 240 days in the 5th year can, per this settled interpretation (as applied in Madras Petrochem and similar rulings), be treated as fulfilling the 5-year requirement
Yes, automatically, regardless of how many days were actually worked in the final year
No, because gratuity requires exactly 5 complete calendar years with zero exceptions
questions.src: Payment of Gratuity Act 1972, Section 2A — defines 'continuous service' such that 240 days worked in the 12 months preceding the relevant year counts as a full year of continuous service; this interpretation (applied in cases like the Madras High Court's Mettur Beardsell rulings and similar) is a well-known nuance distinguishing it from a naive 'exactly 5 full years' reading
